strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of existing CLIP-based FER methods for subtle expressions
Strong empirical results on BioVid and StressID datasets with consistent improvements over state-of-the-art CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablation studies on temporal module design, window length, prompt templates, and AU adapter impact
Sensible approach using Action Units as structured prompts that provide interpretable and anatomically grounded representations of facial expressions
Practical method that requires neither AU ground-truth annotations nor additional labeled data for personalization at test time
Clear presentation with well-designed figures illustrating the method and comprehensive supplementary materials with additional results
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (AU prompting from prior work, established entropy minimization for TTA, straightforward temporal windowing) rather than introducing fundamentally new methodological contributions

Significant experimental limitations undermining generalization claims: only 10 target subjects per dataset for personalization evaluation, no statistical significance testing, no confidence intervals, and high variance across subjects

Severe performance degradation on BAH dataset (69.8 WAR/41.1 F1) reveals fundamental limitation for ambivalent expressions; paper acknowledges but does not adequately address this limitation where AU patterns lack stability

Methodological concerns: (1) circular reasoning risk where window selection based on AU-video alignment then uses selected windows for AU tuning; (2) entropy minimization edge cases (uniform/multimodal distributions) not analyzed; (3) AU ground-truth validation against OpenFace is visual-only without quantitative correlation

Missing experimental rigor: no cross-dataset evaluation (e.g., train on BioVid, test on StressID), no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (learning rate, iteration count), no ablation on entropy minimization loss vs. alternatives

Incomplete justification for design choices: why 46 AUs specifically, no ablation on different AU set sizes, limited theoretical grounding for why AU prompts fundamentally outperform semantic class descriptions

Limited scope reduces impact: only three subtle emotion datasets (pain, stress, ambivalence), unclear performance on macro-emotions or diverse expression types; binary classification setup (neutral + target emotion) oversimplifies the problem

Statistical validation absent: subject-wise results show 50-100% performance range with no error bars, significance tests, or confidence intervals; personalization stability questionable with only 10 subjects per dataset
Reproducibility concerns: critical details in supplementary materials, hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored, no code available at review time, unclear data split procedures

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing personalization in subtle emotion recognition for healthcare applications
Sensible use of AU descriptions as structured semantic prompts offering better interpretability than generic class prompts
Comprehensive experimental comparisons with recent CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines
Consistent empirical improvements across three datasets with reasonable margins
Systematic ablation studies examining temporal module design, window selection, and AU components
Interpretable approach with AU activation visualization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (AU prompts + standard entropy minimization TTA) without significant innovation
Critically insufficient experimental validation: only 10 target subjects per dataset without statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals—inadequate for firm conclusions

Questionable practical utility: per-video test-time adaptation with parameter reset is memorization-like behavior rather than true personalization; requires unlabeled full test videos and 10 optimization iterations per video

Unjustified core assumption: lacks rigorous explanation for why CLIP embeddings should naturally align AUs with emotional dynamics; AU prompting novelty is limited to straightforward prompt substitution
Severely limited scope: only 3 niche emotions (pain, stress, ambivalence) with no evaluation on standard benchmarks (AffectNet, FER2013) or cross-dataset generalization studies
Unfair baseline comparisons: image-level TTA methods adapted to video, T3AL from action recognition; no comparison with traditional AU-based methods or non-CLIP approaches
Incomplete validation: OpenFace validation is circular (another detector, not ground truth); claims of improved AU agreement not rigorously quantified
Methodological concerns: severe class imbalance (BAH: 50% UAR), several subjects at 50% performance floor unexplained, BAH F1 only 41.1% suggesting fundamental applicability limits

strengths: Well-motivated integration of Action Units as structured textual prompts within CLIP, providing fine-grained facial semantics suited to subtle expressions
Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets with consistent improvements and extensive comparisons against CLIP-based and TTA baselines
Practical design requiring no AU supervision, with lightweight architecture and subject-specific personalization without additional labeled data
Thorough ablation studies examining temporal module design, prompt templates, AU vs. class prompts, and robustness to subject pool size
Strong quantitative results on BioVid (81.5% WAR) and StressID (80.8% WAR) with detailed subject-wise analysis showing personalization benefits
Good reproducibility practices with promised code release and comprehensive supplementary materials including AU lists and implementation details
Interpretability through AU visualizations and t-SNE analysis demonstrating improved class separation and alignment with external AU detectors
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: core components (entropy minimization, AU-video similarity, 1D-CNN) are established; contribution is primarily combinatorial rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Limited scope to subtle emotions only (pain, stress, ambivalence); no evaluation on basic emotions, raising serious generalization questions
Modest improvements on realistic/challenging data: BAH (most natural dataset) shows only ~2% improvement over T3AL, with F1 scores remaining low at 41.1%, indicating poor per-class balance

AU supervision claim is overstated: despite claiming 'no AU supervision,' method uses hand-crafted FACS descriptions requiring substantial domain knowledge; no ablation on description quality or alternatives

Test-time adaptation scalability concerns: unclear how method handles multiple test videos per subject, video interleaving, or computational cost; per-video adaptation then reset is operationally unclear

Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single runs reported; subject-level performance shows high variability (50-100% range) without variance quantification
Missing key comparisons: no comparison with recent AU detection methods, multi-task learning approaches with AUs, or other fine-grained recognition methods beyond CLIP variants
Fundamental limitations with ambivalent expressions explicitly acknowledged but inadequately addressed; method struggles when subjects express contradictory AU combinations
AU adapter architecture minimally specified (just '2-layer MLP'); sensitive design choice inadequately justified with insufficient ablation
Prompt engineering under-explored: AU descriptions are terse; no systematic study of verbosity, detail level, or alternative formulations; CLIP's known sensitivity to phrasing not leveraged

strengths: Well-motivated use of Action Units as structured text prompts for capturing fine-grained facial expressions, with clear advantages over generic emotion labels or LLM-generated descriptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three healthcare datasets with extensive comparisons to CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines, demonstrating consistent improvements
Thorough ablation studies validating each component (temporal module, prompt templates, window selection, AU adapter) with detailed analysis
Practical test-time personalization addressing subject-specific expression variability without requiring AU annotations
Computational efficiency: achieves best performance with substantially fewer parameters and lower computational cost than competing methods
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and comprehensive supplementary materials (15 pages) including additional results and extended ablations
Qualitative validation via AU visualizations (Figure 4) showing improved alignment with external AU detector
Subject-wise results demonstrating stability across individual subjects despite high overall variance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (AU prompts, temporal modeling, entropy-guided selection, prompt tuning) are straightforward applications of existing techniques; contribution is primarily combinatorial rather than conceptually novel

Narrow application scope restricted to health-related subtle emotions (pain, stress, ambivalence) with limited generalization evidence; FERV39K evaluation shows notably lower performance (47.3 vs. 78.0 WAR on BioVid)
Small test sets (10 subjects per dataset) make results sensitive to subject selection; some subjects achieve 100% accuracy across methods suggesting potential data biases

Test-time adaptation reliability concerns: entropy minimization alone can suffer from confirmation bias; no mitigation strategies or failure mode analysis; requires test-time video access limiting practical applicability
AU ground-truth validation relies on external detector (OpenFace) rather than dataset annotations, raising questions about detector reliability for subtle expressions and potential circular reasoning
Hand-crafted AU prompts lack systematic exploration of prompt engineering sensitivity; phrase vs. sentence-level ablation shows modest 3-4% difference
Missing comparisons with other AU-aware emotion recognition methods and domain adaptation approaches specifically designed for FER personalization
Incomplete failure analysis: BAH results consistently show low F1 (~40%), indicating method struggles with ambivalent expressions, but this is only briefly acknowledged without in-depth investigation
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals in main paper; robustness analysis only in supplementary materials with limited random seed sampling
Window length selection (16 frames) appears somewhat arbitrary despite claims of insensitivity; performance varies 5+ WAR points across window lengths
